social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife and two children

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Blurred vision bilaterally — loss of taste. Bilateral subtle facial weakness. Mild dysarthria.
neurological_exam.motor: Symmetric lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 3/5, knee extension 3+/5, ankle dorsiflexion 3/5. Cannot stand without support. Upper extremity 4/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Temperature sensation loss below T4 level — patchy. Pain and light touch relatively preserved distally. Circumoral numbness.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Diminished bilateral patellar and Achilles (1+). Trace bilateral biceps. Plantars downgoing.
neurological_exam.coordination: Limb ataxia — finger-nose dysmetric bilaterally. Heel-shin ataxic.
neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 2.4 L (predicted 4.0 L — 60%). NIF: -30 cmH2O. Sensory loss pattern initially appeared to have a T4 level on temperature testing — raising concern for cord lesion. However, subsequent detailed exam shows patchy rather than sharp demarcation, more consistent with large-fiber neuropathy. URI with macrolide antibiotic treatment several days prior to onset.

patient.chief_complaint: Sudden temperature sensation loss followed by progressive lower limb instability, weakness, diplopia, and circumoral numbness — preceded by URI.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. B. is a 41-year-old civil engineer presenting with a 10-day history of progressive neurological symptoms. He had an upper respiratory tract infection approximately 12 days ago, treated with a macrolide antibiotic, which resolved. On the day symptoms began, he noticed a sudden loss of hot and cold sensation while taking a shower. He then developed progressive instability and weakness in both legs over the following days. He also developed diplopia, blurred vision in both eyes, and lost his sense of taste. He notes circumoral numbness. By day 7 he could no longer stand without support and presented to the emergency department. On initial exam, a temperature sensory deficit appeared to have a T4 level, which prompted emergent MRI spine. He has no bowel or bladder dysfunction and no incontinence. He has no back pain. He has no history of prior neurological symptoms. Serological testing reveals positive IgM antibodies for multiple viruses including CMV, HSV, and EBV — this triple seropositive pattern raised concern for a primary viral meningoencephalitis.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: CRP 18.2 mg/L (H), ESR 54 mm/hr (H), CMV IgM Positive (titer 1:80) (H), EBV VCA IgM Positive (titer 1:40) (H), HSV IgM Positive (titer 1:20) (H).

findings.finding: DML 7.2 ms (prolonged); CV 28 m/s (severely reduced); CMAP 2.4 mV (reduced)
DML 7.8 ms (prolonged); CV 26 m/s (severely reduced); CMAP 2.0 mV
R1 response absent; R2 response delayed (delayed blink reflex) — consistent with proximal facial nerve demyelination

quantitative_data.pattern: Severe mixed demyelinating polyneuropathy with conduction block; absent F-waves all nerves — acquired demyelinating (AIDP) electrodiagnostic pattern

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study. 1. Markedly prolonged distal motor latencies bilaterally (peroneal 7.2 ms, tibial 7.8 ms, median 6.4 ms). 2. Severely reduced motor conduction velocities bilaterally (peroneal 28 m/s, tibial 26 m/s, median 38 m/s) with reduced CMAPs. 3. Absent sural SNAPs bilaterally; severely reduced median SNAP (6 µV). 4. Absent F-waves all nerves bilaterally; absent H-reflex bilaterally. 5. Delayed blink reflex: absent R1, delayed R2 — indicating proximal facial nerve conduction slowing. Pattern consistent with severe mixed demyelinating polyneuropathy with conduction block

ecg.interpretation: Sinus tachycardia with borderline prolonged QTc (458 ms)

cardiac_monitoring.rhythm_summary: Sinus rhythm with sustained sinus tachycardia, mean rate 104 bpm
findings: Baseline rhythm on the admission ECG: Sinus tachycardia at 104 bpm, QTc 458 ms
Persistent sinus tachycardia, rate 104 bpm at rest, sustained on the recording — the commonest autonomic manifestation in this disease and, on its own, not an indication for intervention
QTc 458 ms carried over from the admission ECG and unchanged on the recording — relevant to the choice of any QT-prolonging drug during the admission
No bradyarrhythmia, no pause beyond 2 seconds, no AV block and no sustained tachyarrhythmia over the monitored period
cardiac_monitoring.impression: Continuous inpatient telemetry through the period of maximal weakness. Autonomic involvement affects about two thirds of patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome and is a leading cause of in-hospital death, so this recording is a monitoring requirement rather than a diagnostic test: what it looks for is the bradyarrhythmia, the pause beyond 3 seconds and the blood-pressure lability that trigger ICU escalation, alongside serial respiratory function. Sustained sinus tachycardia is documented. It is the mildest and most frequent autonomic sign here, requires no treatment in itself, and is monitored because it often precedes the bradyarrhythmias that do. Beyond the rate, the recording is normal. That is the expected result in this patient and it is not a wasted test: the value of monitoring in this disease lies in what it excludes during the window in which dysautonomia can appear.

general.summary: No directly applicable, high-quality evidence was retrieved for this query. Recommend correlating with current society guidelines.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, severe AIDP with sensory ataxia (post-URI)

differential.key_features: Sensory predominance and ataxia; serology (SSA/SSB) and onconeural antibodies; pure sensory neuronopathy typically lacks demyelinating EMG.
Ataxia + areflexia overlap; absence of ophthalmoplegia argues against classic MFS; anti-GQ1b useful.
Cannot exclude at <8 weeks; reassess longitudinally.
Subacute, chronic; B12 level and methylmalonic acid testing; areflexia possible but CSF protein and demyelinating EMG redirect to GBS.
MRI excludes structural cause; sensory level absent.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, CMP, HIV, anti-GM1/anti-GQ1b ganglioside antibodies, and stool culture / Campylobacter serology if recent diarrhea
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild leukocytosis / elevated inflammatory markers reflecting antecedent infection; ganglioside antibodies for variant typing; trigger identification (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV)

optimal_actions.action: Order nerve conduction studies and needle EMG (EMG/NCS)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Demyelinating pattern (prolonged DML, conduction block, reduced CV, absent F-waves) consistent with AIDP, or reduced CMAP amplitudes in axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN)

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Albuminocytologic dissociation — elevated protein with cell count <10/μL; may be normal in the first week of illness

optimal_actions.action: Order bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) and repeat every 4–6 hours
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline and serial FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF; deterioration to FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP worse than -30 cmH2O, or VC <40% predicted triggers ICU transfer / intubation

optimal_actions.action: Search the medical literature for IVIG vs plasma exchange evidence to guide disease-modifying therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days) and plasma exchange are equivalently effective first-line therapies; combination not superior

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions / contraindications for IVIG (renal function, IgA deficiency screen) and/or plasma exchange (coagulation, calcium, hemodynamics)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirmation that IVIG can be given safely (no severe renal impairment, no IgA deficiency) or that plasma exchange is appropriate (adequate vascular access, stable coagulation)

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for autonomic dysrhythmias and baseline QTc
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus tachycardia or bradycardia; conduction or repolarisation abnormalities reflecting autonomic involvement

optimal_actions.action: Start continuous inpatient cardiac telemetry for the period of maximal weakness and keep it running alongside serial respiratory function. Autonomic instability affects about two thirds of patients and is a leading cause of in-hospital death: bradyarrhythmias, pauses beyond 3 seconds and blood-pressure lability are what trigger ICU escalation
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sustained sinus tachycardia at 104 bpm with no bradyarrhythmia, no pause beyond 2 seconds and no AV block: the mildest autonomic manifestation, and a recording whose value is in excluding the arrhythmias that would escalate care

useless_tools.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

critical_actions: Continuous cardiac telemetry for autonomic features.
Send ganglioside panel and consider paraneoplastic / Sjögren serology if presentation atypical.
contraindicated_actions: Do not delay treatment awaiting full antibody panels.
Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy.
key_reasoning_points: Sensory-ataxic GBS variant exists; elevated CSF protein and demyelinating EMG anchor the diagnosis.
Sensory ataxia raises differentiation with paraneoplastic / Sjögren ganglionopathy — broader serology when atypical.
